Learning Objectives
Specify the structure of native articular cartilage and its maintenance.
Specify the biology of cartilage graft, repair, and restoration options.
Understand the clinical application of various cartilage treatment modalities.
Articular Cartilage Structure, Maintenance, and Injury
Structure
Cartilage is an avascular, alymphatic, and aneural structure in adults.
Nutrients diffuse through the matrix from the surrounding synovial fluid, the synovium, or the
underlying bone.


Structure
Articular cartilage mainly consists of extracellular matrix (ECM, 95%) and a sparse
population of chondrocytes (5%), which maintain the ECM throughout life. The major
three components of articular cartilage ECM are water, collagen, and proteoglycans.
Water constitutes 65% to 80% of articular cartilage and is contained in the ECM. The
frictional resistance of the water through the pores of the ECM and the pressurization of
the water within the ECM are the basic mechanisms by which articular cartilage derives
its ability to support very high joint loads.
Collagen constitutes more than 50% of the dry weight of articular cartilage and 10% to
20% of the wet weight and provides shear and tensile strength. Most collagen (90% to
95%) in articular cartilage is type II collagen. Other minor types of collagen in articular
cartilage include type V, type VI, type IX, type X, and type XI (Table 1).

Proteoglycans constitute only 10% to 15% of the dry weight of cartilage but provide
abundant compressive strength by trapping water. Proteoglycans are produced by
chondrocytes. Two major proteoglycan subtypes include chondroitin sulfate and keratan
sulfate. Proteoglycans primarily help determine movement and management of ECM
water.
Chondrocytes represent 5% of the wet weight of articular cartilage and are the only cells
found in articular cartilage. Chondrocytes are responsible for the production,
organization, and maintenance of the ECM. Mesenchymal cells aggregate and
differentiate into chondroblasts, which remain in lacunae to become chondrocytes.
Chondrocytes produce collagen, proteoglycans, and other proteins found in the ECM.
In addition, articular cartilage has distinct layers that can be divided into different zones
that are based on the depth of cartilage depending on collagen orientation, chondrocyte
organization, and proteoglycan distribution. These include the superficial (tangential or
zone I), the middle (transitional or zone II), the deep (radial or zone III), and the calcified
(zone IV; Figures 1 and 2).

Cartilage Maintenance and Injury
Synovium tissue and synovial fluid support articular cartilage.
Cartilage has a limited ability to heal itself or generate new native articular cartilage.
Evidence of injury to articular cartilage is encountered during 60% to 65% of routine knee
arthroscopic procedures.1 Nearly one-half of professional basketball players (47.5%) have
asymptomatic cartilage lesions observed on MRI.2
The repair of articular defects is limited by a lack of vascularity and a lack of cells that can
migrate to injured sites.
Proteoglycan mass and size decrease with aging in articular cartilage.
A decrease in the concentration of chondroitin sulfate occurs with aging.
An increased concentration of keratan sulfate occurs with aging.
Protein content increases with aging.
Water content decreases with aging.

Cartilage Maintenance and Injury
Synovial tissue is vascularized tissue that mediates the diffusion of nutrients between
blood and synovial fluid. Fibroblast-like cells produce synovial fluid. Synovial fluid is
composed of an ultrafiltrate of blood plasma and fluid produced by the synovial
membrane. The fluid is composed of hyaluronic acid, lubricin, proteinase, collagenases,
and prostaglandins. Lubricin is the key lubricant of synovial fluid. The viscosity coefficient
of synovial fluid is not a constant; its viscosity increases as the shear rate decreases.
Hyaluronic acid molecules behave like an elastic solid during high-strain activities. In
addition, synovial fluid contains no red blood cells, hemoglobin, or clotting factors.
Elastohydrodynamic lubrication is the major mode of lubrication of articular cartilage.
The coefficient of friction of human joints is 0.002 to 0.04. The following decrease this
coefficient of friction: fluid film formation, elastic deformation of articular cartilage, and
synovial fluid. In addition, the fibrillation of articular cartilage increases friction.

Cartilage lacks undifferentiated cells that can migrate, proliferate, and participate in the
repair response. Therefore, cartilage defects have a well-defined limited ability to heal
spontaneously and often worsen over time. Superficial lacerations that do not cross the
tidemark (the region between uncalcified and calcified cartilage) generally do not heal.
Chondrocytes proliferate near the site of injury and may synthesize new matrix, but they
do not migrate toward the lesion and do not repair the defects. The poor healing
response is believed to be partly because of the lack of hemorrhage and the lack of an
inflammatory response necessary for proper healing.
Deeper cartilage lacerations that penetrate past the tidemark into underlying
subchondral bone may heal with fibrocartilage, which is a tissue produced by
undifferentiated marrow mesenchymal stem cells that later differentiate into cells
capable of producing fibrocartilage. Unfortunately, in most patients, the repair tissue
does not resemble the normal structure, composition, or mechanical properties of an
articular surface and is not as durable as hyaline cartilage.
As humans age, multiple changes in articular cartilage composition and metabolism
occur. The immature articular cartilage present at birth differs considerably from adult
articular cartilage. With aging, chondrocytes become larger, acquire increased lysosomal
enzymes, and no longer reproduce. Cartilage becomes relatively hypocellular in
comparison with immature articular cartilage. As age advances, cartilage loses its
elasticity, developing increased stiffness and decreased solubility.
Biology of Articular Cartilage Treatment Options
Overview
Articular cartilage defects are graded according to the modified International Cartilage Repair
Society grading system3 (Figure 3):
Grade 0: normal appearing cartilage
Grade I: superficial lesions with fissures and cracks
Grade II: lesions extending to less than 50% of cartilage depth
Grade IIIa: lesions extending to more than 50% of cartilage depth
Grade IIIb: defects extending to the calcified layer

Grade IIIc: defects down to but not through the subchondral bone
Grade IIId: delamination
Grade IV: osteochondral defects and lesions extending through the subchondral bony
surface
Goals of treatment strategies for the management of articular cartilage defects are to deliver
or provide cells or tissue that may repair and/or regenerate cartilage within and adjacent to
cartilage defect sites.
Management of articular cartilage injuries includes nonsurgical and surgical treatment options.
Surgical treatment options include stabilization, reparative, restorative, and alternative
procedures.
After nonsurgical or surgical management of articular cartilage lesions, healing can be
evaluated via the International Cartilage Repair Society histology grading system after biopsy,
using a histologic evaluation of the following categories:4,5
Surface
Matrix
Cell distribution
Cell population viability
Subchondral bone
Mineralization

osteoarthritis. The International Cartilage Repair Society (ICRS) grading system for chondral
lesions in osteoarthritis is based on the arthroscopic appearance of the cartilage surface as
(grade 0) normal, (grade I) nearly normal, (grade II) abnormal, and (grade III, grade IV) severely
abnormal as determined by lesion depth. In addition, late-stage osteoarthritis (OA) is
characterized by complete loss of cartilage and subchondral bone sclerosis. Symptomology of OA
is primarily managed via a combination of pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions
until partial or total joint replacement is necessary; however, clinical guidelines may vary. IA =

regeneration, replacement, and substitution, in Aaron RK, ed: Orthopaedic Basic Science:

2021, pp 415-432.)

Overview
Nonsurgical treatment modalities include rest, activity modifications, nonsteroidal anti-
inflammatory medications, physical therapy, corticosteroid injections, and
viscosupplementation. Patients may present in any one of these stages, and surgical
treatment is only offered on failure of or inability to comply with the aforementioned
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000000
8/20

treatment progression. Pain control and shock absorption are the primary goals of the
nonsurgical management of articular cartilage defects. However, the definitive
management of articular cartilage lesions often is not possible without surgical
intervention given the structural compromise of cartilage tissue inherent to these
injuries.
Stabilization Procedures

Stabilization Procedures
These procedures do not rely on any healing of cartilage lesions and often are
performed as adjunctive techniques; however, they are critical in preventing cartilage
lesion propagation, destabilization, and progression. Stabilization procedures aim for the
débridement of articular cartilage lesions and generally are performed via arthroscopic
means. The simple débridement of articular cartilage lesions is used as the primary
treatment option for the management of lesions that only involve less than 50% of the
cartilage thickness. Therefore, cartilage lesions graded as International Cartilage
Regeneration Society grade I (superficial lesions, fissures, cracks) or grade II (lesions
extending down to <50% of cartilage depth) usually are managed via these means for
definitive management in patients in whom nonsurgical treatment fails.
However, stabilization procedures also are used as adjunctive treatment options in
combination with various other surgical interventions for the management of articular
cartilage lesions. For example, if a surgeon plans to use osteochondral allograft plugs or
perform autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI) at a later date for the management
of a known defect, débridement of deep cartilage lesions may help stabilize a lesion
from propagating further during planning stages of future procedures. In addition, given
that patients with articular cartilage defects often have undergone several prior
surgeries, stabilization procedures may be performed in combination with any other
procedure and help prevent future progression. However, if the subchondral plate is not
disrupted and marrow elements do not communicate with the surface of the cartilage

defect, no inflammatory stage will occur, and fibrocartilage formation (a reparative
procedure response) should not be expected.
Reparative Procedures or Marrow Stimulation Techniques to Stimulate
Tissue Growth in a Débrided Cartilage Lesion
These techniques have a limited ability to generate new and native hyaline cartilage with type
II collagen
Microfracture
Subchondral drilling
Abrasion arthroplasty

Reparative Procedures or Marrow Stimulation Techniques to
Stimulate Tissue Growth in a Débrided Cartilage Lesion
Microfracture and subchondral drilling rely on releasing undifferentiated stromal cells
from the subchondral bone underlying the cartilage lesion along with growth factors
from the subchondral bone to simulate a vascular healing response or scar (Figure 4).
An angiogenic healing response is initiated during this process that leads to defect
repair.6 In addition, the use of platelet-rich plasma also has been used to encourage
healing.7,8 This environment includes platelets, white blood cells, cytokines, and growth
factors that may aid in cartilage defect repair.9
The primary tissue formed from these techniques is a fibrocartilaginous scar.10,11 This
scar is formed after marrow elements are allowed to move into the defect. This scar
tissue helps stabilize the cartilage defect; however, it has inferior ability to withstand the
compressive and shear loads compared with native articular cartilage. In addition, the
resulting fibrocartilage often has limited amounts of type II collagen and is primarily
composed of type I collagen. Commercially-available products that include bio-scaffolds
may be used to stabilize the scar or clot formed after marrow-stimulation.

Cell-based techniques involve three major phases: harvesting (biopsy, often
arthroscopically and of a non–load-bearing cartilage surface), cell isolation and culture
expansion, and implantation (open or arthroscopically; Figures 5 and 6). Usually, the
biopsy must include 200 to 300 mg of cartilage tissue. This cell-based treatment for the
management of cartilage defects primarily uses a patient’s own chondrocytes for
cartilage restoration. Cells are expanded in a commercial laboratory in vitro and then are
reintroduced into a patient’s articular environment via various approaches. Although the
goal is a healed surface consisting of hyaline-like articular cartilage, results are variable.
Evidence suggests that cell-based techniques generate hyaline cartilage only in a
minority of patients, with a mixed fibrohyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage surface
generated in most patients.12 In addition, other problems with cell-based techniques
include graft hypertrophy or overgrowth, damage to surrounding cartilage from
implantation techniques, uneven cell distribution, and graft delamination.13

Figure 5 Illustration shows preparation and implantation of autologous chondrocytes in
first- to fourth-generation therapies. Autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI)
techniques involve a two-stage process of (1) isolation and preparation of autologous
chondrocytes and (2) subsequent implantation. Initially, cartilage is harvested, and the
chondrocytes are isolated, expanded, and prepared (A) as a liquid cell suspension (for
first- or second-generation ACI) or a cell-seeded scaffold (for third- or fourth-generation
ACI). Implantation of first- or second-generation ACI involves preparation of the defect
(B), periosteal harvest (for first-generation ACI) (C), suturing of the periosteum or
collagen membrane over the defect, application of fibrin glue, and implantation of
chondrocytes as a liquid cell suspension. Implantation of third- or fourth-generation ACI
involves placement of a cell-seeded scaffold and adherence with fibrin (without
membrane coverage). (Reproduced from, Gacasan EG, Sah RI: Articular cartilage repair:
Augmentation, regeneration, replacement, and substitution, in Aaron RK, ed:

Four major generations of cell-based techniques exist. First-generation procedures have
largely been abandoned with the development of newer generation procedures but
generally included products such as autologous cultured chondrocytes for implantation.
In first-generation ACI, the harvested and expanded chondrocytes are implanted under a
periosteal flap sewn in place over the cartilage defect. Second-generation ACI involves
the use of collagen membranes specifically designed for implantation over expanded
chondrocytes. Third-generation ACI (such as matrix-induced ACI) involves the use of a
collagen or hyaluronic acid scaffold on which chondrocytes are seeded rather than
expanded in a liquid medium. Ultimately, this scaffold is implanted after the expansion
phase. Cellular concentrations range from 0.5 to 3.0 × 106 cells per cm3. Fourth-
generation ACI typically involves the use of more advanced culture methods and
scaffolding systems. This system involves the use of a scaffold with expanded

chondrocytes that were grown in an environment of pressure and hypoxia to improve
cell proliferation and matrix production.14
Osteochondral autografting (osteochondral autograft transfer system or mosaicplasty)
usually is limited to smaller articular cartilage lesions (<2 cm2; Figures 6 and 7). This
process is associated with the advantages of replacing the cartilage surface with healthy
autograft cartilage from a non–load-bearing area. In addition, this tissue also is
supported by an attached subchondral bony plug to support the transplanted articular
cartilage. This process quickly restores normal biomechanical properties lost in patients
with a full-thickness articular cartilage defect.
Figure 7 Illustration shows osteochondral grafting techniques. Depending on the size of
the defect, osteochondral lesions may be managed with the use of osteochondral
autografts or osteochondral allografts. Autologous grafts, consisting of single or multiple
(mosaicplasty) plugs, generally are used to resurface focal defects that are 1 to 4 cm2.
Osteochondral allograft transplantation involves the transfer of size-matched tissue
from a cadaver model donor into defects larger than 2 cm2, with the type of allograft
dependent on lesion size and severity. (Reproduced from Gacasan EG, Sah RI: Articular
cartilage repair: Augmentation, regeneration, replacement, and substitution, in Aaron

RK, ed: Orthopaedic Basic Science: Foundations of Clinical Practice, ed 5. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 415-432.)
Although these autografts often are used in patients with smaller lesions, they may be
used in patients with a lesion larger than 2 cm2. In these patients, multiple plugs are
incorporated using predetermined sizing systems. If autografts are overlapped with one
another, small unfilled areas or clefts are created. These clefts often are filled with a
fibrocartilaginous response.15 However, on histologic analysis, the transplanted
autograft retains its hyaline cartilaginous structure after transplantation.15
Similar to the osteochondral autograft transfer system, osteochondral allografts involve
the implantation of an intact articular surface supported by a subchondral bone plug.
However, this process involves the use of donor allograft tissue that is size-matched
from cadaver bone/cartilage surfaces, typically a hemi-distal or whole distal femoral
condyle, trochlea, patella, or tibial plateau.
Processing of osteochondral allograft tissue is critical to successful outcomes. Prolonged
storage and freezing may result in graft degradation, cartilage fissuring and
delamination, and eventual chondrocyte death.16 In addition, bone marrow elements
from healthy donors are removed via various methods depending on the tissue bank.16-
18 The bony plug under the cartilaginous portion of the implant serves as an
osteoconductive host for the patient’s normal bony elements to in-grow and ultimately
replace with host bone via a process known as creeping substitution.19 This process has
been shown to primarily occur only at the most superficial surfaces of the donor bone
and, therefore, the subchondral bony thickness should be kept to the minimum
necessary to support the donor articular cartilage surface.20 However, even after
successful incorporation and healing, most remaining allograft tissue is dead bulk
bone.21 Regardless, allograft cartilage cells have demonstrated persistent viability at
more than 2 years after implantation, and allograft osteochondral transfer success often
is attributed to this prolonged viability of donor chondrocytes.22

Cell-based Therapies
Autologous mesenchymal stem cell implantation
Induced pluripotent stem cells
Embryonic stem cells

Cell-based Therapies
Various other cell-based alternative therapies are being developed that involve various
cell lines found in bone marrow or other sources and ultimately are differentiated into
articular cartilage. These therapies may be used to augment existing cell-based
therapies, such as ACI, or as wholly new approaches for the management of articular
cartilage defects. Many such cell-based therapies derive cells from bone marrow or
adipose tissue.23,24 In addition, a chondrogenic environment may be supported by
biochemical stimuli, such as transforming growth factor beta, fibroblast growth factor,
bone morphogenic protein, and insulin-like growth factor. These various adjunctive
techniques are supported by preclinical animal studies but are not currently approved
by the FDA.
Scaffold-based Strategies

Scaffold-based Strategies
Scaffold-based strategies attempt to mechanically restore articular cartilage surface
function with the use of osteochondral scaffolds in the absence of cellular tissue. The
ultimate goal of these osteoconductive scaffolds is to allow bone growth and integration
into the scaffold with host articular cartilage tissue. These matrices rely on the successful
local migration of chondrogenic cells and growth factors to formulate an articular
cartilage-like surface; preliminary results are mixed.25,26
